title: Alien Draft Seal Transparent Silicone Weather Stripping Review
text: No more cold drafts? That's the promise, but let's see what this silicone strip actually does for a typical winter home. I’m unboxing three rolls that total roughly 49 feet, all clear and flexible, ready for a DIY seal job. Winter weather drives a lot of us to hunt for ways to keep our houses warm without cranking the furnace. Alien’s Draft Seal is a transparent silicone flap, about 1.4 inches wide and 0.19 inches thick, backed with adhesive. The package comes with three rolls, together giving roughly forty nine feet of clear silicone, so you can tackle several openings in one go. The package includes three rolls, each roughly 16.34 feet long, so you can cut to fit several windows or doors. Each roll measures about sixteen point three four feet long and one point four inches wide, letting you cut precise lengths for each gap. The material is flexible, which the brand says helps it follow the contour of frames without creasing. According to the brand, the silicone stays flexible and resists creasing even after repeated opening and closing of doors. Because it’s clear, the strip aims to blend in with wood, glass, or metal surfaces, staying out of sight. The adhesive backing is described as moisture-resistant, though you’ll still want a clean, dry surface for the best hold. Adhesive backing means no screws or special hardware—just measure, cut, and press onto a clean surface. It’s marketed for wood, glass and metal frames, so check that your window or door material matches one of those surfaces. When you apply it, the flap sits against the gap, creating a thin barrier rather than a bulky stopper. A quick tip: wipe the area with a lint-free cloth, then let it dry before pressing the strip on. The hands-on footage shows a cut piece being pressed onto a window frame, the adhesive feeling tacky but not messy. Measure the gap first, then add a tiny margin for the flap to sit flush without compressing the frame. The seal relies on a good surface; glossy glass or dusty frames can weaken the adhesive hold. If the gap is deeper than the strip’s one point four inch width, you may need a thicker weather-stripping solution. It won’t fix damaged frames or large, irregular openings—those need more robust repairs. The adhesive may struggle on glossy glass or oily surfaces, so those areas might need a different sealing method. Because it’s thin, a mis-cut piece could interfere with a door’s swing or a window’s latch. When cutting, a sharp pair of scissors gives a clean edge, reducing the chance of the strip peeling later. If you’re a homeowner or renter with small drafty gaps around windows, doors, or sliding doors, this could work. Renters who can’t drill holes often appreciate this stick-on approach, as long as they follow the surface prep steps. People who prefer a low-profile, invisible solution will appreciate the transparent silicone design. Homes with severely warped frames or large, irregular openings will likely need more robust repair than a thin silicone flap can provide. Skip it if you have severely damaged frames, oversized gaps, or surfaces that the adhesive won’t stick to. Also avoid it if you need a freestanding draft stopper or expect guaranteed energy-bill reductions. Overall, the Alien Draft Seal offers a flexible, clear strip that’s easy to cut and stick for modest gaps. It’s best suited for DIY winter weatherproofing where aesthetics matter, but it won’t replace proper insulation or major repairs.
